1. It’s Black. It’s all black. One solid chunk of blackness. Any cookware made of cast iron should be heavy and black. You don’t get any plastic handles or painted-on logos. Anything written on cast iron is stamped into the metal and will last forever. Which brings me to my second point:

  2. It Lasts For-Fucking-ever I could take my favorite Skillet and throw it out the window, leave it out there for 20 years, dig it up and season it and it’d be safe to cook on*. There’s no part of cast iron that can “break”. I have put a skillet through some very tough thermal shock and never had a problem. You can take it camping with you and use it to hammer in tent poles. The worst thing that can happen is that you ruin the “seasoning” on it but...

  3. You Can Fix it Yourself Good luck trying to reapply teflon to your 3-year-old pan that you just forgot was on the burner. Also enjoy the cancer you just got from whatever was vaporized. Looks like it’s time to go out and buy a new $50 pan and make sure you’re up to date on your health insurance premiums, dumb ass. Next time use cast iron, which loves the high heat and just needs a nice little oil-rub to be ready to go again. I’m pretty sure even YOU can figure that one out.

  4. It’s Science Now don’t get all scared on me. This isn’t going to be on your GED exam. I’m not even going to use big words like “polymerization” because I want all of you to keep reading. There’s a lot of cool information out there about cast iron and how it heats up and transfers heat to the food. There’s even more interesting stuff out there about exactly what “seasoning” is and how it works. I love all that stuff but you don’t HAVE to know it. All you have to know is:

  5. You Cook with High Heat Turn that fucking flame up. If you don’t hear that high-heat sizzle when you slap a sirloin on your griddle, then be assured you just ruined your dinner. Cornbread should sizzle when you pour the batter into the skillet because the skillet should be hot. I have cast iron bread pans that get preheated with the oven before I butter them up and pour the batter in. Cast iron cookware should always be hot. The rule in our house is that if there is cast iron cookware on the stove, assume it’s hot until proven otherwise.

  6. The Perfect Steak is done on Cast Iron It follows logically that if the manliest food out there is steak, and the best way to cook a steak is on cast iron, then cast iron must be the manliest way to cook.

I’m sure that I will get detractors who will claim that an open flame is clearly the manliest way to cook. But I disagree. It is too primal and uncontrolled. Cast iron takes the power of the open flame and directs it towards its one purpose. Like a gun controlling an explosion to fire a bullet, a cast iron skillet controls a flame to create delicious food.

*This is not true if you live in an irradiated waste-land. If you do live in irradiated waste-land then I assume that your bunker doesn’t have any windows and that you won’t be alive for 20 more years.

Kosher Salt and a paper towel. I'll put about a teaspoon of kosher salt in the pan right after I'm done using and quickly wipe it down. It can be really hot, so sometimes I'll use tongs to hold the paper towels but usually I wipe quickly enough that the paper towels don't get too hot. What're your thoughts on this, this is what I do with mine:

  1. Rinse pan with hot water, this is to remove excess grease and oil in the pan (but not ALL of it)

  2. Rinse pan with cold water, basically to get rid of the hot water. Hot/warm water from a tap is more likely to have nasties in it brought up from the pipes (This might not be scientific but it's the reason why I never use hot tap water to cook with)

  3. Wipe pan down with paper towel

  4. Oil that baby up.

Alternatively to step 1, drain the oil/grease into a small container through a coffee strainer. Use this oil/grease to rub down the pan (after rinse & wipe) then discard of any excess. Might be a touch unhealthier, but you're going to be getting that fuck HOT before you cook on it next, aren't you? AREN'T YOU?!

I have a friend that just waves a paper towel above the skillet and calls it clean. He swears it makes everything taste better but it seems gross to me. As long as you're using the pan regularly and not storing for long periods with obvious food chunks in it, I think minimal cleaning is fine.

If a wipe doesn't suffice, hot water to clear off excessive oils followed by a bold water rinse. Germs are more likely to froth at the loins in a warm pan that is resting, a cold pan is less likely to harbour germs. When you get hot water from the tap there is a higher chance that the temperature will have brought any of the (unlikely) nasties on the tap walls with it, so a final rinse with cold is always good. Wipe down with paper towel after the rinse. Edit: Oh! And oil it up baby yeah. As @jbi said, salt and paper towel work well. When you put detergent on it you are basically destroying any accumulated flavours in the pan. To me, each piece of cast iron cookware should have its own flavour, built up over many uses and embedded in the pan and the memories you share with it.
